T1.label: Sulphide intrusion, gated by light
T1.text: Eelgrass detoxifies sediment sulphide by leaking oxygen from its roots into the rhizosphere - radial oxygen loss, the same mechanism wetland plants use. That leak is powered by photosynthesis. Under low light it weakens, sulphide enters the roots and rhizome, and the plant is poisoned from below.

T2.label: Loss of the sulphide-detoxifying symbiosis
T2.text: Seagrass beds host lucinid clams whose gill bacteria oxidise sulphide, keeping the rhizosphere habitable. Plant, clam and bacterium are a three-way partnership.

T3.label: Wasting disease with stress-modulated virulence
T3.text: *Labyrinthula zosterae* destroyed most Atlantic eelgrass in the 1930s and is still present. Virulence depends on host condition: plants under low light, heat or sulphide stress are far more susceptible.

T4.label: Marine replant failure: negative sediment feedback
T4.text: Restoration plantings fail in sediment whose chemistry looks adequate - the marine form of replant disease. Candidate causes are the accumulated pathogens, the missing symbionts of T2, the lost binding of D8, and autotoxic residues.

T5.label: Loss of sediment suppressiveness
T5.text: Some soils suppress disease purely through their microbial community, and suppressiveness is transferable - mix 1-10% of a suppressive soil into a conducive one and it becomes suppressive. Anaerobiosis and fumigation destroy it.

V1.label: Deficiency
V1.text: A required input falls below what is needed. Energy, an element, light, an edible particle, a vitamin, a service performed by something else.

V2.label: Excess and toxicity
V2.text: An input exceeds what can be tolerated - including too much of a required thing. Shelford's ceiling, not Liebig's floor.

V3.label: Condition outside the envelope
V3.text: A physicochemical field - temperature, salinity, pH, redox, pressure, hydrodynamic energy - moves outside the range the organism tolerates. Distinct from V2 because it is a state, not a substance arriving.

V4.label: Mechanical destruction and burial
V4.text: Structure removed, crushed, smothered, abraded or mobilised. No chemistry required at any point.

V5.label: Biotic attack
V5.text: Predation, grazing, disease, parasitism, competition, invasion. Something else does the killing.

V6.label: Loss of a partner or a performed function
V6.text: The organisms whose activity the focal organism depends on are gone - symbionts, facilitators, and the ones that were conditioning the environment for everyone.

V7.label: Failure to replace itself
V7.text: The population dies without any individual being killed: no propagules, no connectivity, no settlement cue, wrong timing, too little genetic variation. **The register was almost empty here until the avenues were written down.**

V8.label: Rate exceeded
V8.text: The change is survivable in magnitude but not in speed. Adaptation, acclimation, migration and recovery all have rates, and a disturbance returning faster than recovery completes is a different thing from the same disturbance once.

M1.label: Depletion of something essential
M1.text: Anything life requires falls below what some part of the community needs. Oxygen is the famous instance and the only one the requirement acts on, but it is an instance: silicon, light at the bed, carbonate ion, cobalamin, thiamine, available iron and edible particles of the right size all belong here, and group K works through them. **A depletion is selective, not general** - it removes whoever needed the missing thing and releases whoever did not.

M2.label: Toxic exposure
M2.text: Something is poisoned. The dose makes the poison, so this route is acutely sensitive to peak concentration rather than to any annual mean — and annual means are what is reported. Leaves a fully oxygenated dead water.

M3.label: Physical destruction and burial
M3.text: The habitat removed, crushed, dredged or covered. Needs no chemistry at all.

M4.label: Food-web restructuring
M4.text: Removal or addition of a species changes what everything else does. Overfishing, invasion, disease.

M5.label: Light starvation
M5.text: Rooted vegetation shaded out by turbidity, which then removes the thing that was holding the sediment down.

M6.label: Surface film and gel
M6.text: The water itself becomes a different medium: greasy, foaming, mucilaginous.

M7.label: Reduced chemistry at the bed
M7.text: Sulphide and its relatives, toxic in their own right and an oxygen sink besides. The bed becomes hostile before the water column shows anything.

M8.label: Failure of renewal
M8.text: The population is not killed; it fails to replace itself. No propagules, no connectivity, no settlement cue, wrong timing, or too few left to find each other. Every individual can be healthy and the population still ends.

M9.label: Change faster than response
M9.text: The magnitude is survivable and the rate is not. Acclimation, adaptation, migration and recovery all take time, and a disturbance that returns before recovery completes is a different thing from the same disturbance once.

U1.label: Mixture and cocktail effects
U1.text: Toxicity is assessed one substance at a time against one threshold at a time. Real exposure is simultaneous, and effects combine additively at best and synergistically often. The number of pairs alone, let alone higher orders, exceeds what could ever be tested. There is no defensible way to compute the combined effect, and equally none to argue it is zero.

U2.label: Acute peaks under chronic means
U2.text: The dose makes the poison, and the dose that kills arrives in an event. Monitoring reports means over months; an outfall discharging for six hours after a storm is invisible in an annual average and entirely visible to whatever was living below it.

U3.label: Floor and ceiling effects
U3.text: Where a community has already lost its sensitive members, adding stress produces no further measurable change — so the most degraded places return the smallest effect sizes, and a naive analysis reads that as evidence the stressor does not matter.

U4.label: Substances on no monitoring list
U4.text: Tens of thousands of chemicals are in commerce; a few dozen are measured. A substance absent from the list is absent from every finding, whatever it is doing.

U5.label: Sublethal and transgenerational effects
U5.text: Impaired reproduction, behaviour and development leave no corpse to count. The survey counts individuals present, not individuals functioning.

O1.label: Oxygen deficit
O1.text: Dissolved oxygen below 4 or 2 mg/L, by depth, duration and extent. **An observable on route M1, not an outcome.** Nobody values a gas concentration; it earns its place only through what it causes, and it is neither necessary nor sufficient for any of T1-T5.

O2.label: Fedtemøg
O2.text: Greasy organic matter in the water and on the shore. It has at least three manifestations and they are not the same measurement: **O2a** accumulation at the waterline, a transport-and-deposition outcome; **O2b** the greasy film on skin after swimming, which is a property of the water column and of the sea-surface microlayer, present without any shore deposit and reported at different times of year; **O2c** the smell, which is a chemical signature (sulphide, amines, volatile fatty acids) and the thing the public actually reports. Denmark measures none of the three.

O3.label: Loss of higher benthic life
O3.text: The large, slow, long-lived animals going. Reachable by suffocation, poisoning, burial or physical destruction.

O4.label: Turbidity and phytoplankton biomass
O4.text: Chlorophyll and light attenuation. Measures of quantity, standing in for claims about composition.

O5.label: Foam
O5.text: Persistent foam on the water and along the strandline. A surfactant and protein phenomenon, and a different measurement from either greasiness or shore deposit.

O6.label: Mass mortality events
O6.text: Fish kills, and die-offs of any other conspicuous group. Sudden, dateable, and the clearest possible evidence that *something* happened — reachable by hypoxia, toxin, pathogen or heat.

O7.label: Loss of rooted vegetation
O7.text: Eelgrass and macroalgal depth limit and cover. The WFD's own biological indicator, and the one that has conspicuously failed to recover as loads fell.

O8.label: Visible discolouration
O8.text: Water turned brown, red or milky. What people photograph and report, and what the chlorophyll indicator averages away.

O9.label: Bathing water failure
O9.text: Closures and quality downgrades. The one outcome Denmark measures densely, over a long period, at 1,026 points.

A.label: Nutrient-driven production in place
A.text: Nutrients arrive, something grows, it dies, its decay consumes oxygen. The official hypothesis is A1; the rest of the group are its siblings and are treated no differently.

B.label: Oxygen demand that arrived already made
B.text: Organic matter imported ready to decay. No growth step, and for most of the group no nitrogen at any point.

C.label: Physical control of resupply
C.text: Oxygen deficit is a balance. Half of it is whether the water is refilled.

D.label: Physical disturbance of the bed
D.text: Reduced sediment brought into contact with oxygen, and the fauna removed mechanically.

E.label: Chemical demand and toxicity
E.text: Oxygen consumed by chemistry rather than biology, and life removed by poison rather than by suffocation. One thing governs the toxic half of the group and is worth stating before any of it: **a biocide's molecular target is almost always ancient and shared.** Selectivity is a matter of dose, uptake and metabolism, not of the target being absent elsewhere. Azole fungicides inhibit the sterol enzyme CYP51, which every eukaryote has. Strobilurins block complex III of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, and SDHIs block complex II, which is also a Krebs-cycle enzyme - so both are respiratory poisons for anything that breathes. Neonicotinoids act on acetylcholine receptors and pyrethroids on sodium channels, both universal in animals, and for these purposes a copepod is an insect. Triazine herbicides block photosystem II, which is what an alga photosynthesises with. Glyphosate's target is absent in animals but present in plants, bacteria and fungi, which makes it an antimicrobial. Naming a compound after the taxon it is sold to kill describes the market, not the biochemistry.

F.label: Biological structure and feedback
F.text: What the community itself does to the water, and what its loss stops doing.

G.label: Climate and long-term drivers
G.text: Slow forcings that change the baseline every other hypothesis sits on.

H.label: State, memory and regime
H.text: Hypotheses in which the current year's drivers are not the explanation.

J.label: Surface film, gel and the greasy water itself
J.text: Fedtemøg as a property of the water rather than of the shore. These are the mechanisms that produce a greasy film on skin, and they are the ones that can operate in a sea with no Danish catchment at all.

K.label: Depletion and imbalance of what life requires
K.text: The policy frame is that there is too much of something. The plant-nutrition literature is about there being too little, and about ratios. Liebig's law of the minimum says growth is set by the scarcest essential resource, not by the sum; Shelford's law of tolerance says every requirement has a ceiling as well as a floor; and horticultural antagonism says an excess of one nutrient *induces deficiency* of another by blocking its uptake. Under those three, "too much nitrogen" and "depleted of something else" are not opposite diagnoses. They are the same one.

W.label: Renewal and rate
W.text: A population can end without anything killing an individual, and a system can fail at a magnitude it would survive if it arrived more slowly. This group exists because the categorical avenues had two entries - failure to replace itself, and rate exceeded - with almost nothing under them in a register of 127. That absence was not a judgement that these do not matter; nobody had thought to look.

Z.label: The physical fields and their windows
Z.text: Light starvation is the same argument as chemical deficiency, one physical layer up - and the layer behaves differently in a way that matters. A chemical has one axis: how much. A field has several, and each carries its own floor and ceiling. Light is not only how much, but of what wavelengths, for how long, and when. So the exhaustive treatment of the physical avenue is a small cross-product - the fields are enumerable, their dimensions are enumerable, and each dimension admits exactly the same three failure modes as a chemical does. This is the most nearly closable part of the whole register, and among the least examined.

T.label: Sediment sickness: symbionts, pathogens and why nothing grows back
T.text: Horticulture has a name for ground where a plant will not grow although the nutrients are adequate: replant disease, or soil sickness. Its causes are biological - accumulated specialist pathogens, autotoxic exudates, and the loss of the symbionts and the suppressive microbial community that made the plant resilient. The sea has the same thing, it has been documented largely by Danish researchers, and it does not appear in the assessment because the assessment measures the medium's chemistry and not its biology.

S.label: The land side: the medium, not the input
S.text: Retention - the fraction of applied nutrient that never reaches the sea - is the largest single number in the whole account, and GEUS state it *"kan i praksis ikke måles direkte"*. It is a property of soil and hydrogeology, and soil properties vary over metres. The tropical-soil literature is the cautionary case: phosphate fixation by iron and aluminium oxides in Ferralsols and Andosols is the *same reaction* as the marine sediment phosphate trap, and seventy years of work on it has produced a vocabulary - sorption capacity, saturation, occlusion, hysteresis - that marine assessment does not use.

R.label: Decay, and the community that does it
R.text: Decomposition ecology has spent a century on the question this project is asking: what happens when organic matter arrives faster than it can be processed, and what breaks when the processors go. Almost none of it appears in marine nutrient policy, which treats decay as a rate constant. It is a relay of organisms, and relays stall. The soil and horticultural literature is the better guide here, and the one difference that does not transfer - the sulphate reservoir - turns out to explain why marine anoxia is a different and worse thing than freshwater anoxia.

L.label: The baseline and the counterfactual
L.text: Not rival causes of degradation, but rival accounts of whether the degradation and its remedy are correctly specified at all. The reference condition is a *modelled* state, and the target is derived from it, so an error there moves every requirement in the country without touching a single measurement. This is the failure mode that took African desertification research thirty years to find: Fairhead and Leach's forest patches in Guinea, read by colonial and successor science as relics of a destroyed forest, had been created by the villagers. The causal arrow was backwards, and the error was in the assumed original state.

I.label: Observation and measurement
I.text: Rival explanations for an apparent trend that live in the instrument rather than the sea. Omitting these is not neutrality; it is an assumption.

A1.label: Danish land-based nitrogen load
A1.text: Waterborne N from Danish land reaches a coastal water, is taken up in summer when N limits growth, the biomass sinks, and its remineralisation draws down bottom oxygen.

A2.label: Phosphorus load
A2.text: P drives the spring bloom, whose sinking biomass sets the organic pool that the summer deficit draws on.

A3.label: Atmospheric deposition on the sea surface
A3.text: Reactive N deposited directly onto the water, bypassing every catchment and every retention term.

A4.label: Point-source discharge of nutrients
A4.text: Treatment plants and industry discharging N and P directly.

A5.label: Advected nutrients from outside Denmark
A5.text: Baltic outflow, German, Swedish and Polish rivers, and North Sea water carrying nutrients into Danish areas.

A6.label: Submarine groundwater discharge
A6.text: Nitrate-bearing groundwater entering the sea beneath the shoreline, counted in no catchment budget.

A7.label: Sediment nutrient regeneration
A7.text: The bed releasing stored N and P back into the water in summer, often supplying most of what primary production consumes.

A8.label: Marine aquaculture
A8.text: Net-pen fish farms discharging dissolved nutrients and particulate feed and faeces directly to the water column and the bed beneath.

A9.label: Nitrogen fixation
A9.text: Cyanobacteria fixing atmospheric N, adding nitrogen the load account cannot see and which increases when N is scarce relative to P.

B1.label: Combined sewer overflow
B1.text: Rain overwhelms a combined system and raw sewage discharges directly: organics, fat, faecal solids, at 1 g O₂ demand per g COD.

B2.label: Separate stormwater
B2.text: Road and roof runoff carrying organics, hydrocarbons, tyre wear and metals through a pipe that was built to skip treatment.

B3.label: Treatment plant organic load
B3.text: Continuous discharge of residual COD and BOD from 750 plants.

B4.label: Riverine particulate organic carbon
B4.text: Soil, plant material and manure-derived carbon washed off land and delivered as particles that decay in the receiving water.

B5.label: Industrial organic discharge
B5.text: Slaughterhouses, dairies, fish processing and breweries discharging high-strength organic effluent.

B6.label: Harbour and fish-processing waste
B6.text: Fish waste, bilge, and organic debris concentrated in enclosed basins with poor exchange.

B7.label: Shipping discharges
B7.text: Sewage, greywater, food waste and scrubber washwater discharged legally under MARPOL along shipping lanes.

B8.label: Direct manure and slurry entry
B8.text: Spills, tank failures, over-application before rain, and field drains carrying slurry to a watercourse.

C1.label: Stratification strength
C1.text: A density boundary that cuts the bottom water off from the atmosphere.

C2.label: Wind work
C2.text: Mixing energy that breaks stratification and re-ventilates the bottom.

C3.label: Residence time
C3.text: How long water and its cargo stay before being flushed.

C4.label: Baltic inflow events
C4.text: Dense saline pulses through the Belts that both ventilate deep basins and strengthen stratification above them.

C5.label: Freshwater discharge buoyancy
C5.text: River flow stratifying the surface independently of what it carries.

C6.label: Water temperature and solubility
C6.text: Warmer water holds less oxygen and respires faster: roughly −2.3% saturation per °C, and demand rising with Q10.

C7.label: Bathymetry, sills and depth
C7.text: Basins below a sill cannot ventilate laterally whatever the wind does.

C8.label: Constructed change to circulation
C8.text: Bridges, tunnels, causeways, reclamation, harbour works and wind farms altering exchange - the Øresund link, Storebælt, Lynetteholm, Nordhavn.

C9.label: Sea level and tidal change
C9.text: Changed exchange volume through straits and over sills.

D1.label: Bottom trawling
D1.text: Gear dragged across the bed destroys structure and fauna directly, and resuspends reduced sediment whose sulphide consumes oxygen on contact.

D2.label: Navigation dredging
D2.text: Channel maintenance removing the bed and suspending it.

D3.label: Dredged-material dumping
D3.text: Sediment, and whatever is in it, deposited at 114 licensed grounds.

D4.label: Sand and gravel extraction
D4.text: Removal of the bed itself at 305 licensed areas.

D5.label: Cable and pipeline works
D5.text: Trenching across the bed for power, data and gas.

D6.label: Anchoring and propeller wash
D6.text: Shallow-water disturbance concentrated in anchorages and approaches.

D7.label: Storm-driven resuspension
D7.text: Waves stirring the bed in shallow water, releasing reduced material and moving deposited organics shoreward.

D8.label: Loss of biostabilisation, and the mobile bed
D8.text: Benthic diatoms and cyanobacteria secrete extracellular polymer that glues the sediment surface, raising the critical erosion threshold by a measured factor of two to five. It is the marine homologue of desert biocrust - the fragile living skin that holds an *erg* still - and it is destroyed by the same thing: surface disturbance.

D9.label: Fertility islands lost to homogenisation
D9.text: Desert vegetation traps sand and concentrates nutrients into mounds with barren interspace - a two-phase mosaic where almost all the biological activity is in a small fraction of the area. Mussel beds, tube-worm fields and eelgrass do the same on a seabed.

D10.label: Winnowing and armouring
D10.text: Currents remove fine sediment and its organic matter, leaving a coarse lag - the marine desert pavement. The bed that remains has different chemistry, different permeability and different fauna.

D11.label: Stabilisers against destabilisers
D11.text: Burrowing fauna destabilise sediment; microphytobenthos and tube-builders stabilise it. Which side dominates decides whether the bed is erodible at all, and the two respond differently to every stressor in this register.

E1.label: Sulphide oxidation
E1.text: Reduced sulphur from anoxic sediment consuming 2 g O₂ per g S the moment it meets oxygenated water.

E2.label: Nitrification demand
E2.text: Ammonium oxidised to nitrate, consuming 4.57 g O₂ per g N with no biology of interest in between.

E3.label: Iron and manganese oxidation
E3.text: Reduced metals from sediment consuming oxygen on contact.

E4.label: Methane oxidation
E4.text: Methane from anoxic sediment consuming 4 g O₂ per g on its way up.

E5.label: Direct chemical oxygen demand of discharges
E5.text: Reduced chemicals discharged in industrial or municipal effluent.

E6.label: Biocides and antifoulants
E6.text: TBT historically, copper and modern boosters now, killing benthic life directly at oxygenated sites.

E7.label: Pesticides and degradation products
E7.text: Agricultural chemicals reaching the sea and acting on non-target organisms, including the algae the indicators count.

E8.label: Pharmaceuticals and personal care products
E8.text: Continuous low-dose exposure from treatment plant effluent, which is not designed to remove them.

E9.label: PFAS and persistent novo-chemicals
E9.text: Compounds with no degradation terminus accumulating in biota and sediment.

E10.label: Heavy metals
E10.text: From harbours, industry, dumping and historic contamination.

E11.label: Ammonia toxicity
E11.text: Un-ionised ammonia toxic to fauna at concentrations well below those that matter for growth, and more toxic as pH and temperature rise.

E12.label: Hydrogen sulphide toxicity
E12.text: Sulphide toxic to fauna in its own right, and the source of the smell people actually report.

E13.label: Biocides that remove the decomposers themselves
E13.text: Not toxicity in general, but toxicity aimed at the guild whose job is to break organic matter down. Fungicides are applied by the thousand tonnes and are designed to kill fungi; fungi are the organisms that degrade the tough fractions - lignin, chitin - that bacteria leave behind.

E14.label: Veterinary antiparasitics in manure
E14.text: Avermectins given to livestock pass through the animal and remain active in its dung. Dung from treated cattle is measurably slower to break down because the insects that break it down are killed by the residue - documented since the 1980s.

E15.label: Total biocide load, whatever its source
E15.text: Household, agricultural and industrial biocides reach the same water and act on the same organisms. Antifoulants, wood preservatives, agricultural fungicides and insecticides, disinfectants, veterinary products, and the antibacterials in ordinary consumer goods.

E16.label: Conserved targets: "selective" is a claim about dose
E16.text: The molecular machinery agricultural biocides attack is shared far beyond the taxon on the label. Azoles inhibit CYP51, the sterol enzyme of every eukaryote, and other cytochrome P450s including the vertebrate ones that make steroid hormones. Strobilurins block respiratory complex III and SDHIs block complex II, which is simultaneously a Krebs-cycle enzyme - conserved wherever there are mitochondria. Neonicotinoids act on acetylcholine receptors and pyrethroids on voltage-gated sodium channels, both universal in animals. Triazines block photosystem II, which is what algae photosynthesise with.

E17.label: The microbiome is the exposed organ
E17.text: Animals and plants carry the target taxa inside them. A fungicide reaching a marine invertebrate meets that animal's fungal and bacterial symbionts; a shikimate-pathway herbicide meets its gut bacteria. The host's own cells may be untouched while the organisms it depends on are not.

F1.label: Loss of filter feeders
F1.text: Mussel and oyster beds clearing the water column; their removal leaves the phytoplankton uncleared.

F2.label: Loss of bioturbators
F2.text: Burrowing fauna irrigate the sediment and oxygenate its upper layer; without them the bed goes anoxic sooner and stays.

F3.label: Loss of eelgrass and macroalgae
F3.text: Rooted vegetation produces oxygen, stabilises sediment and competes for nutrients; its loss removes all three at once.

F4.label: Trophic cascade from a removal far away
F4.text: Removing one level releases the next and suppresses the one below that. The Baltic case is documented: cod were fished down through the 1980s and 90s, sprat were released, their grazing suppressed the large copepods, and the system moved into a state that has not reverted. Cod and sprat now appear to hold each other in alternative stable configurations.

F5.label: Invasive species
F5.text: Comb jelly, Pacific oyster, round goby and others restructuring the food web.

F6.label: Jellyfish blooms
F6.text: Gelatinous predators removing zooplankton and depositing rapidly-decaying biomass.

F7.label: Harmful algal blooms specifically
F7.text: Toxin-producing species killing fauna directly, distinct from biomass.

F8.label: Microbial shift to fast-growing forms
F8.text: When the slow, large and long-lived are gone, what remains are the organisms that turn nutrient into biomass fastest and decay fastest.

F9.label: Disease and parasite mass mortality
F9.text: A pathogen killing a dominant species, leaving a decaying mass.

F10.label: Vertebrate mass mortality
F10.text: Seal, bird or fish die-offs depositing large local organic loads.

F11.label: Viral lysis and the viral shunt
F11.text: Marine viruses run to about ten million particles per millilitre and lyse a large share of the bacterial and algal standing stock every day. Lysis does not pass carbon up the food chain - it returns it to dissolved and colloidal organic matter, to be respired by bacteria again. That short-circuit is the viral shunt.

F12.label: The micropathogens nobody catalogues
F12.text: Viruses, bacteria, protists, fungi and oomycetes cause mass mortality in marine organisms routinely - eelgrass wasting, sea star wasting, oyster herpesvirus, crustacean and bivalve pathogens. The set of possible attackers is bounded by the biota, but the catalogue is worst exactly at the small end.

G1.label: Warming
G1.text: Less oxygen held, faster respiration, stronger and longer stratification - three effects in the same direction.

G2.label: Changing precipitation and runoff timing
G2.text: More intense rain moves the same annual load into fewer, larger events, and drives more overflow.

G3.label: Changing wind climatology
G3.text: Less storminess or a shift in direction reducing mixing in the critical season.

G4.label: Acidification
G4.text: Lower pH impairing calcifying fauna, and shifting the ammonia equilibrium toward the toxic form.

G5.label: Changing ice cover
G5.text: Less winter ice changes both winter ventilation and the spring bloom timing.

G6.label: Sea level rise
G6.text: Changed exchange volumes and altered shallow-water dynamics.

H1.label: Alternative stable states and hysteresis
H1.text: The system has more than one self-maintaining configuration, and having been pushed into the degraded one it stays there at load levels that would never have caused it.

H2.label: Sediment legacy
H2.text: The organic pool accumulated over decades sets the current deficit; this year's load is a small increment on it.

H3.label: Loss of resilience through diversity loss
H3.text: A simplified community absorbs less disturbance, so the same stress now produces a collapse it once would not have.

H4.label: Subsidy-stress
H4.text: The same nutrient is a subsidy at low dose and a stressor at high, so the response is non-monotone and a linear coefficient is the wrong shape.

J1.label: Transparent exopolymer particles and marine gel
J1.text: Phytoplankton and bacteria exude sticky polysaccharide gel - TEP - especially under nutrient imbalance, when cells fix carbon they cannot balance with N or P and dump the excess as extracellular carbon. The gel aggregates into marine snow and, at scale, into mucilage.

J2.label: Sea-surface microlayer enrichment
J2.text: The top micrometres of the sea concentrate surfactants, lipids, proteins and hydrophobic pollutants by orders of magnitude over the bulk water, and convergence lines concentrate that film further.

J3.label: Surfactants from detergents and personal care
J3.text: Anionic and non-ionic surfactants passing through treatment plants and storm outfalls, which are surface-active by design and accumulate in the microlayer.

J4.label: Sunscreen and UV filters
J4.text: Oily and silicone-based personal care products applied directly by bathers and delivered at the exact place and season people swim.

J5.label: Microplastic and its biofilm
J5.text: Particles that carry a biofilm and sorb hydrophobic organics, concentrating in the same surface film.

J6.label: Oil and hydrocarbon films
J6.text: Operational discharges, bilge, road runoff and scrubber washwater leaving thin films that spread over large areas from small volumes.

J7.label: Exudate from senescing blooms
J7.text: A bloom that is dying releases far more dissolved and colloidal organic carbon than a bloom that is growing.

J8.label: Bacterial exopolymer from fast-growing communities
J8.text: When the large and slow are gone, what remains are r-selected bacteria that produce copious extracellular polymer.

K1.label: Silicon depletion and the diatom-to-flagellate shift
K1.text: Diatoms build frustules of silica and cannot grow without dissolved silicon. Si comes from rock weathering, so human activity does not raise it, while N and P have risen severalfold. When Si runs out first, diatoms are replaced by flagellates and cyanobacteria - poorly grazed, prone to harmful blooms, and the principal producers of the gel in group J. Enhanced production also buries Si faster, so the depletion reinforces itself.

K2.label: Stoichiometric imbalance decides who grows
K2.text: Redfield C:N:P at 106:16:1 and roughly Si:N at 1:1 for diatoms are requirements, not averages. Skewing the ratios changes which organisms can complete their life cycle, independently of how much of anything there is.

K3.label: Macronutrient excess inducing micronutrient deficiency
K3.text: Standard horticultural antagonism: high nitrogen suppresses uptake of copper and boron, high phosphorus induces zinc deficiency, high potassium blocks magnesium and calcium. The excess starves the organism of something else.

K4.label: Thiamine (B1) deficiency
K4.text: Thiamine deficiency causes mass mortality of fry and adults; Baltic salmon M74 syndrome is documented from the 1970s onward, and similar deficiency has been implicated in bird and fish die-offs across the region.

K5.label: Cobalamin (B12) and cobalt limitation
K5.text: Most algae cannot make vitamin B12 for themselves and have to get it ready-made from bacteria — they are *auxotrophs* for it. The vitamin, and the cobalt at its centre, is a limiting resource produced by one part of the community for another.

K6.label: Iron bioavailability
K6.text: Iron is required for photosynthesis and nitrate reduction. Coastal water is usually iron-replete in total, but availability depends on redox state and on organic ligands, both of which change with hypoxia and with organic loading.

K7.label: Carbonate ion depletion
K7.text: Acidification is usually framed as pH falling. For a calcifying organism the operative quantity is the depletion of carbonate ion and the fall in aragonite and calcite saturation - a resource being removed, not a toxin arriving.

K8.label: The narrow window between deficient and toxic
K8.text: Copper, zinc, manganese, nickel, selenium and boron are all essential and all toxic, often within an order of magnitude. Shelford's law of tolerance, in the elements.

K9.label: Selenium
K9.text: Required for the glutathione peroxidase system, protective against mercury, and toxic in modest excess. Deficiency has been implicated in fish and bird mortality elsewhere.

K10.label: Salinity change and osmotic cost
K10.text: The Danish straits are a salinity gradient, and every organism in them sits near an edge of its tolerance. Changing freshwater delivery or Baltic inflow moves the whole community's position in that range.

K11.label: Light as a depleted resource
K11.text: Distinct from turbidity as a symptom: for a rooted plant, light at the bed is a resource with a hard requirement - roughly 11-14% of surface irradiance for eelgrass - and below it the plant does not grow slowly, it dies.

K12.label: Loss of habitat-forming structure
K12.text: Mussel beds, eelgrass, stone reefs and biogenic structure are a resource in themselves - surface, refuge, and hydrodynamic shelter. Denmark's stone reefs were physically removed for construction stone through the twentieth century.

K13.label: Food depletion for filter feeders and larvae
K13.text: Filter feeders and larvae need the right particles in the right size range at the right time. A shift from diatoms to picoplankton or gel can leave high chlorophyll and nothing edible.

K14.label: Genetic and functional diversity depletion
K14.text: Repeated mortality events select the survivors down to a narrow set, and a narrow set has fewer ways to respond to the next disturbance.

T6.label: Enrichment dissolving the partnership
T6.text: High phosphorus suppresses mycorrhizal colonisation: a well-fed plant stops maintaining the symbiosis that was feeding it and protecting its roots.

T7.label: Anaerobic phytotoxins other than sulphide
T7.text: Waterlogged soil generates organic acids, ethylene, and reduced iron and manganese at toxic concentrations - a suite of phytotoxins well known in agronomy and distinct from oxygen shortage itself.

T8.label: Anaerobic conditions select the pathogens
T8.text: Oomycetes - the Pythium and Phytophthora group - swim as zoospores, need water, and thrive where roots are stressed and oxygen is low. Marine oomycetes and labyrinthulids exist and are barely studied.

R11.label: Marine fungi, the decomposers nobody counts
R11.text: Fungi are the principal degraders of refractory material on land - lignin, chitin, cellulose - and the reason a forest floor does not simply accumulate. Marine fungi exist, are diverse, degrade the same recalcitrant fractions, and are absent from essentially every marine monitoring programme including Denmark's.

S1.label: Retention is a property of the medium and varies by an order of magnitude
S1.text: Denmark is split between sandy glacial outwash in western Jutland - low clay, low organic matter, low exchange capacity, high leaching, the Arenosol case - and clayey moraine in the east. The same application leaches very differently from each.

S2.label: Phosphorus saturation, and legacy leakage
S2.text: Sorption sites are finite. Degree of phosphorus saturation is already used in Dutch and Danish regulation, and soils in high-livestock areas are saturated after decades of manure. Past that point, applied P goes straight to runoff.

S3.label: Sorption is hysteretic - a ratchet on the land side too
S3.text: Phosphate enters the sorbed and occluded pools far more readily than it leaves. In the most weathered soils occlusion is effectively irreversible.

S4.label: Total is not available
S4.text: Soil science distinguishes resin, bicarbonate, hydroxide, acid and residual phosphorus pools by sequential extraction, because total P says almost nothing about what an organism can get. Marine sediment P is generally reported as a bulk total.

S5.label: Buffering scales with the volume of reactive medium
S5.text: The Leptosol lesson: a soil under 25 cm deep has almost no capacity to absorb a shock, because buffering is proportional to the volume of material doing the buffering.

S6.label: Retention capacity is saturable, so the coefficient is not constant
S6.text: Retention is treated as a fixed fraction. If the mechanisms behind it - denitrification capacity, sorption sites, organic matter - are finite and have been loaded for decades, the fraction falls over time.

L6.label: The degraded bed is classified as its own habitat type
L6.text: A chronically trawled seabed and a naturally sandy one look the same in a sediment sample, and habitat classification records both as sand. The flattened state is then enshrined as a habitat *type* with its own expected community, against which it scores as healthy.

R1.label: The C:N threshold, and fat as a nitrogen sink
R1.text: Decomposer microbes build biomass near C:N 8-10 at about 40% carbon-use efficiency, so there is a threshold near C:N 25: below it decay releases mineral nitrogen, above it decay consumes it. Straw at C:N 80 starves the next crop. Fat has no nitrogen at all.

R2.label: Priming of the old sediment pool by fresh carbon
R2.text: Adding labile carbon to soil accelerates decomposition of the old recalcitrant pool, because the microbes gain the energy to attack the hard fraction. Decades of soil science; not applied to marine sediment in assessment.

R3.label: The decay relay stalls when a stage is removed
R3.text: Decomposition is a relay - leaching, fragmentation by detritivores, microbial catabolism, humification - and removing a link leaves material unprocessed. Australian cattle dung sat on the ground until dung beetles were imported.

R4.label: Nitrogen enrichment retards decay of the recalcitrant fraction
R4.text: Well established in soil: nitrogen accelerates decay of labile litter but suppresses the lignin-degrading enzymes of white-rot fungi, so recalcitrant material decays *slower* under high nitrogen and the persistent pool grows.

R5.label: The terminal electron acceptor cascade, and why salt changes it
R5.text: Decay runs down a ladder of electron acceptors - O₂, then nitrate, then manganese, then iron, then sulphate, then CO₂ - each yielding less energy. Freshwater carries 5-30 mg/L of sulphate and so passes it quickly to methanogenesis. Seawater carries 2,700 mg/L, a hundred to five hundred times more, and sulphate reducers outcompete methanogens for hydrogen and acetate.

R6.label: Sulphide locks the iron that would hold the phosphate
R6.text: Sulphide precipitates FeS, removing the iron oxides that bind phosphate in oxic sediment. A salt-specific step, because freshwater lacks the sulphate to make enough sulphide.

R7.label: Estuarine flocculation deposits river carbon at the coast
R7.text: Dissolved organic matter and clay from fresh water flocculate on meeting salt and drop out of suspension, concentrated in the mixing zone.

R8.label: Lipids are less soluble in seawater
R8.text: Salting-out: dissolved organics, and lipids especially, are less soluble at high ionic strength and partition preferentially into films, aggregates and the surface microlayer.

R9.label: Home-field advantage, and novel material
R9.text: Litter decomposes fastest in the community adapted to it. Material a community has never encountered - novel chemicals, invasive species' tissue, synthetic polymers - decomposes slower and accumulates.

R10.label: Osmotic discontinuity for the decomposers themselves
R10.text: Freshwater and marine decomposer communities are different organisms, and neither functions well in the other's water. The salinity front is a discontinuity in the decomposition machinery, not only in the chemistry.

L1.label: The reference condition never existed
L1.text: Environmental targets are set against a modelled pre-impact state. If that state is wrong - if the coast was never as clear, as vegetated or as oligotrophic as the model supposes - then the gap being closed is partly an artefact of the model rather than a loss.

L2.label: The reference is a model output treated as a fact
L2.text: Denmark's chlorophyll target is computed by ensemble modelling of a reference situation, then scaled by an EU-agreed ratio of 0.6. Both halves are choices, and neither is a measurement.

L3.label: The trend depends on the start year
L3.text: Almost every Danish series begins in the 1970s or later, at or near the historical maximum of nutrient loading. A trend measured from a peak is a recovery; the same data from a different start is something else.

L4.label: Recovery is blocked by something other than the driver
L4.text: A target can be unreachable because a *different* thing is missing - seed stock, substrate, the bioturbators, the iron the sediment lost - while the driver being managed is already at the required level.

L5.label: The reference sites are not references
L5.text: Where the reference is spatial rather than historical - a comparable unimpacted area - the comparison assumes such an area exists. In a sea with no unfished, undredged, undeposited water anywhere, it may not.

W1.label: Propagule supply and connectivity
W1.text: Recolonisation needs propagules to arrive. If the source populations are gone or the currents no longer connect them, a site with perfect conditions stays empty.

W2.label: Settlement cue failure
W2.text: Larvae of many species choose where to settle using chemical and acoustic cues from existing habitat. A degraded bed does not smell or sound like habitat, so larvae that arrive do not stay.

W3.label: Phenological mismatch
W3.text: Larval release, spawning and the spring bloom are timed by different cues - temperature, photoperiod, stratification onset. Warming moves them at different rates, so the food and the mouths that need it drift apart.

W4.label: Allee effects at low density
W4.text: Below a density threshold, reproduction fails - broadcast spawners do not fertilise, mates are not found, group defences stop working.

W5.label: Recovery slower than the disturbance interval
W5.text: A bed trawled every few months, or dredged on a maintenance cycle, is held permanently in early succession. The slow-growing, structure-forming, long-lived species never reach maturity.

W6.label: Change outrunning acclimation
W6.text: Organisms acclimate and populations adapt, and both have rates. A warming or freshening survivable over a century can be lethal over a decade.

W7.label: Too little variation left to respond with
W7.text: Repeated mortality selects survivors down to a narrow genetic and functional set, and a narrow set has fewer ways to meet the next disturbance.

Z1.label: Light: too little, and too much
Z1.text: The floor is the eelgrass requirement, roughly 11-14% of surface irradiance. The ceiling is real too: photoinhibition and UV damage at the surface, which is why some species do worse in the clearest water.

Z2.label: Light quality, not quantity: browning
Z2.text: Water attenuates red first, then blue, and coloured dissolved organic matter shifts the surviving spectrum brown-green. Photosynthetic pigments are tuned to particular wavelengths, so **which** organisms can photosynthesise changes even at constant total irradiance. CDOM export from catchments has been rising across Nordic waters - the browning phenomenon - and it is driven by land use, hydrology and recovery from acidification rather than by nutrients.

Z3.label: Photoperiod and timing as a cue
Z3.text: Day length is a signal as well as an energy supply - it triggers spawning, settlement, germination and migration. Turbidity changes the effective photoperiod at depth without changing the calendar.

Z4.label: Temperature: window, and rate
Z4.text: A floor, a ceiling, and - separately - a maximum rate of change that acclimation can follow. The Danish straits sit at the southern edge for boreal species and the northern edge for others, so both tails are populated.

Z5.label: Hydrodynamic energy has a floor as well as a ceiling
Z5.text: Too much and organisms are dislodged, abraded and buried; too little and filter feeders are not delivered food, larvae are not dispersed, and nothing is flushed.

Z6.label: Sound, as a cue and as a stressor
Z6.text: Larvae of many marine invertebrates and fish orient to reef sound when choosing where to settle. Shipping noise and pile driving mask it, and impulsive noise injures directly.

Z7.label: Electromagnetic fields
Z7.text: Subsea power cables generate magnetic and induced electric fields. Elasmobranchs and some invertebrates use electroreception for navigation and prey detection.

Z8.label: The attenuation budget is never partitioned
Z8.text: Kd is one broadband number. Ocean optics decomposes it as a sum of independent contributions - pure water, phytoplankton pigment, coloured dissolved organic matter, mineral particles, and non-algal detritus - each with its own spectral signature, and the partition is standard practice with a spectroradiometer.

Z9.label: Epiphyte shading, which bypasses the water column
Z9.text: Nutrient enrichment promotes algae growing directly *on* the eelgrass leaf. The host is shaded at the blade surface, where no water-column measurement reaches.

Z10.label: Mineral plumes from works
Z10.text: Dredging, extraction, dumping, cable laying and construction all put mineral particles into suspension. They attenuate light, abrade, and settle on leaves and gills, and none of it involves a nutrient.

Z11.label: The weakened host
Z11.text: Light starvation need not kill directly. A shaded plant photosynthesises less, leaks less oxygen from its roots, carries less reserve, and is then more susceptible to sulphide intrusion (`T1`), to wasting disease whose virulence tracks host stress (`T3`), and to ordinary starvation.

I1.label: Changing station network
I1.text: Stations added, moved and dropped over the record, so a trend can be a trend in where you looked.

I2.label: Changing analytical method
I2.text: Winkler titration to optode sondes for oxygen; changing chlorophyll methods. Different instruments have different biases.

I3.label: Changing sampling frequency and season
I3.text: A deficit indicator built from the worst month is biased by how often you sampled that month. More visits find more extremes.

I4.label: Changing indicator definition
I4.text: The indicator itself was redefined - intercalibration, EQR thresholds, seasonal windows - so a change in status can be a change in the ruler.

I5.label: Changing correction factors
I5.text: The record carries both an original and a corrected result plus the factor applied. Corrections are a modelling choice inside the raw data.

I6.label: Changing custodian
I6.text: The 2007 structural reform moved monitoring from the counties to the state; the raw record names the supplier and the technical instruction used.

acetylcholine.text: The signalling molecule nerves use at many junctions. Its receptors and the enzyme that clears it are targets for several insecticide classes, and both are universal in animals.
acetylcholine.why: Acetyl plus choline, its chemical parts.

aerobe.text: An organism that needs oxygen to live. Most animals, and many bacteria.
aerobe.why: Greek aer (air) plus bios (life). Its opposite is an anaerobe.

AIS.text: Automatic identification system - the transponder ships broadcast for collision avoidance, which incidentally records where everything went.
AIS.why: Designed for safety, useful as an activity archive.

Alcian blue.text: A dye that stains the sticky sugar-based gel algae secrete, which is otherwise transparent. It is the only reason anybody knows the gel is there.
Alcian blue.why: Without it, transparent exopolymer particles are invisible - which is why they went unnoticed until the 1990s.

Allee.text: Below a certain population density, reproduction fails - mates are not found, spawning does not coincide, group defences stop working. The decline then feeds itself.
Allee.why: Warder Clyde Allee, 1930s. The counterintuitive half of population ecology: rarity itself can be the cause of further rarity.

allelopathy.text: One plant chemically suppressing another. Some macrophytes release compounds that inhibit the algae competing with them.
allelopathy.why: Greek allelon (of each other) plus pathos (suffering).

ammonium.text: The simplest form of dissolved nitrogen, the form in sewage and in decaying material. Bacteria oxidise it to nitrate, consuming oxygen; in alkaline water it converts to ammonia, which is acutely toxic.
ammonium.why: From ammonia, ultimately from the temple of Amun in Egypt, near which the salt was collected.

anaerobic.text: Without oxygen - either an environment with none, or an organism that lives without it. Anaerobic decay produces different, often toxic, products.
anaerobic.why: Greek an- (without) plus aer. Anaerobiosis is the state; anaerobes are the organisms.

anammox.text: Bacteria combining ammonium and nitrite directly into nitrogen gas without needing oxygen. Another route by which nitrogen leaves permanently.
anammox.why: Contraction of anaerobic ammonium oxidation. Only discovered in the 1990s.

Andosol.text: A soil formed on volcanic ash. It fixes phosphate more strongly than any other soil type - fertiliser can disappear from availability almost entirely.

anoxia.text: No oxygen at all, as opposed to too little.
anoxia.why: Greek an- (without). The step past hypoxia, and chemically a different world - sulphate reduction takes over.

archaea.text: A third domain of life alongside bacteria and eukaryotes - superficially bacteria-like, biochemically very different, and responsible for much methane and ammonia cycling.

Arenosol.text: A sandy soil: little clay, little organic matter, holds almost no water or nutrients, leaches heavily.
Arenosol.why: Latin arena, sand - the same word as the sand-floored arenas of Rome.

autoclave.text: To sterilise by steam under pressure. Autoclaved material has identical chemistry to the original and no living organisms, which is how you separate a chemical effect from a biological one.
autoclave.why: Greek auto (self) plus Latin clavis (key) - the lid seals itself as pressure rises.

auxotroph.text: An organism that cannot make some essential compound for itself and must obtain it ready-made. Most marine algae are auxotrophs for vitamin B12.
auxotroph.why: Greek auxein (to grow) plus trophe (nourishment): needs feeding to grow.

azole.text: The largest class of agricultural and medical fungicides. They block sterol synthesis at an enzyme every eukaryote shares, so their selectivity comes from dose and uptake rather than from the target being absent.
azole.why: Named for the five-membered nitrogen ring they contain.

Beggiatoa.text: A sulphide-eating bacterium that forms thick white mats on oxygen-poor sediment. Its presence is a visible sign that the bed has gone sulphidic.
Beggiatoa.why: Named after Francesco Secchi di Beggiato, a 19th-century Italian physician.

benthic.text: Of the seabed - the animals, plants and processes on or in the bottom.

benthos.text: Everything living on or in the seabed, taken together.

bicarbonate.text: The dissolved form most of the ocean's carbon takes. Plants can use it for photosynthesis, and it buffers the water against pH change.
bicarbonate.why: The carbonate system's middle state, between dissolved CO2 and carbonate ion.

biocrust.text: A living skin of cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses binding a desert soil surface. Break it and the sand mobilises.
biocrust.why: Biological soil crust. Its marine counterpart is microphytobenthos.

biogenic.text: Made by living things. Biogenic structure means reefs, beds and burrows built by organisms rather than by geology.

biomagnification.text: A substance becoming more concentrated at each step up the food chain, because predators accumulate everything their prey had. Mercury and some organics do this; most metals do not.
biomagnification.why: Distinct from bioaccumulation, which is build-up within one organism over its life.

bioturbation.text: The churning of sediment by animals burrowing, feeding and irrigating their tunnels. It mixes oxygen down into the bed.
bioturbation.why: Bio- plus the same turba: life doing the stirring.

bivalve.text: A shellfish with two hinged shells - mussel, clam, oyster, cockle. Most filter their food from the water, which incidentally clears it.
bivalve.why: Two valves, meaning the two halves of the shell.

BOD.text: Biochemical oxygen demand - the share of COD that microbes will actually consume, usually measured over five days.
BOD.why: The biologically available part of the oxygen demand.

brackish.text: Water between fresh and fully marine. The Danish straits are brackish, and few species tolerate it, so the communities there are unusually species-poor.

bundfauna.text: Danish for seabed animals - the standard term for the soft-bottom fauna survey that is Denmark's main biological measure of seabed condition.
bundfauna.why: Bund is bottom. It is what the ODA topic of that name contains.

carbonic anhydrase.text: The zinc-containing enzyme that lets an organism convert bicarbonate into usable carbon dioxide. Without zinc, photosynthesis is throttled however much carbon is around.
carbonic anhydrase.why: Anhydrase: it removes water from carbonic acid.

CDOM.text: Coloured dissolved organic matter - the brown, tea-like tint that dissolved plant material gives water. It absorbs light, especially blue.
CDOM.why: Its rise across northern waters is called browning, and it is driven by land use and hydrology rather than nutrients.

Charney.text: A feedback where losing vegetation raises the ground's reflectivity, which weakens the rising air that makes rain, which costs more vegetation.
Charney.why: Jule Charney proposed it for the Sahel in 1975. One of the first climate feedbacks anyone wrote down.

chitin.text: The tough material of fungal cell walls and of crustacean and insect shells. After cellulose it is the most abundant biological polymer, and relatively few organisms can digest it.

chlorophyll.text: The green pigment that captures light for photosynthesis. Measuring it is the standard way to estimate how much algae is in the water - it is a proxy for biomass, not for health.

cobalamin.text: Vitamin B12. Built around a cobalt atom, made only by bacteria and archaea, required by most algae.
cobalamin.why: Cobalt plus amine, after the metal at its centre.

COD.text: Chemical oxygen demand - how much oxygen a substance will consume when fully oxidised. Measured in the same units as the oxygen it removes.
COD.why: The measurement and the effect are the same quantity, which is unusual and useful.

copepod.text: A small shrimp-like crustacean, a millimetre or two long, and the main link between algae and fish. Probably the most numerous animal on Earth - and an arthropod, like the insects that insecticides are designed for.

CTD.text: The standard instrument lowered through the water column, recording conductivity, temperature and depth continuously - and usually oxygen too. It gives a profile rather than a single value.
CTD.why: Named for the three things it measures. Salinity is calculated from conductivity.

cyanobacteria.text: Photosynthetic bacteria, often called blue-green algae though they are not algae. Some fix nitrogen straight from the air, which lets them grow when nitrogen is scarce, and several make toxins.

CYP51.text: The enzyme that makes sterols - cholesterol in animals, ergosterol in fungi, phytosterols in plants. Azole fungicides work by blocking it, and every eukaryote has one.
CYP51.why: A cytochrome P450, numbered by family. The number is the only name it has.

denitrification.text: Bacteria converting nitrate to nitrogen gas, which leaves the water permanently. The only process that actually removes nitrogen from a system.
denitrification.why: Undoing nitrification. It needs the nitrate that nitrification makes, so stopping one stops the other.

denitrifying.text: Converting nitrate to nitrogen gas, which removes it from the water permanently. The only process that actually gets rid of nitrogen rather than moving it.
denitrifying.why: Un-doing nitrification. It requires low oxygen and available carbon.

detritivore.text: An animal that eats dead organic material rather than living prey or plants.
detritivore.why: Latin detritus (worn away) plus vorare (to devour).

diatom.text: A single-celled alga that builds itself a rigid glass box out of silica. They need dissolved silicon to grow at all, they are the preferred food of most marine grazers, and they sink fast when they die.
diatom.why: Greek diatomos, cut in two - the shell comes in two halves that fit like a petri dish. The name describes the box, not the organism.

dinoflagellate.text: A single-celled alga that swims with two tails and often wears armour plating. Several make toxins, and some cause red tides.
dinoflagellate.why: Greek dinos, whirling - they spin as they swim.

ecotoxicology.text: The study of how chemicals affect organisms and ecosystems. In regulatory practice it usually means acute mortality tests on a few standard species.
ecotoxicology.why: Ecology plus toxicology - a young field, and its standard methods predate most of what is now known about symbiosis.

eelgrass.text: A true flowering plant that lives fully submerged in the sea, forming meadows on soft bottoms. It roots in the sediment, needs light at the bed, and shelters everything else. Danish: alegras.
eelgrass.why: Named for its long ribbon leaves. Zostera marina is the Danish species.

endocrine disruption.text: Interference with an organism's hormone system, often at concentrations far below those that kill. Effects show as failed reproduction and altered development rather than as death.
endocrine disruption.why: The endocrine system is the hormonal one - Greek endo (within) plus krinein (to separate).

epibenthic.text: Living on the surface of the seabed rather than buried in it.

epiphyte.text: A plant or alga growing on another plant, using it as a surface rather than feeding on it.
epiphyte.why: Greek epi- (upon) plus phyton (plant). On eelgrass they shade the leaf they sit on.

EQR.text: Ecological quality ratio: the observed value divided by the value expected in an unimpacted reference state, scaled so that 1 is pristine.
EQR.why: An EU device for making incomparable national measurements comparable. Its denominator is modelled, not measured.

erg.text: A sand sea - the dune-covered kind of desert, as opposed to stony or salt desert.
erg.why: Arabic 'irq, a dune field. What makes it hostile is that the surface moves, not that it is dry.

eutrophic.text: Over-fed: a water body receiving more nutrient than it can process.
eutrophic.why: Greek eu- (well) plus trophe (nourishment) - literally well-nourished, which is why the word sounds like praise and means the opposite.

eutrophication.text: Over-feeding of a water body: so much nutrient that production outruns what the system can process.
eutrophication.why: Greek eu- (well) plus trophe (nourishment). Literally well-nourished, which is why the word sounds positive and means the opposite.

euxinic.text: Water that is both oxygen-free and carries free sulphide. The worst case.
euxinic.why: From Pontus Euxinus, the Roman name for the Black Sea, whose deep water has been like this throughout recorded history.

exopolymer.text: Sticky long-chain sugars secreted outside the cell. It binds sediment, forms marine gel, and is what makes water feel slippery.
exopolymer.why: Exo- (outside) plus polymer. Marine biologists count it as TEP.

fedtemog.text: Danish, roughly fat-muck: the greasy, foul organic material that accumulates in the water and along the shore. Not a scientific term, and not measured by anything.
fedtemog.why: Fedt is fat, mog is muck or dung. A word from people who swim, not from a monitoring programme.

Feltmåling.text: Danish for field measurement - the ODA category holding instrument profiles taken in the water: CTD casts, light attenuation, oxygen.

Ferralsol.text: A deeply weathered tropical soil dominated by iron and aluminium oxides, which lock phosphate up so tightly that fertiliser vanishes from availability within weeks.
Ferralsol.why: Ferrum (iron) plus aluminium: named for what is left after everything else has weathered away.

flagellate.text: A single-celled organism that swims using a whip-like tail. In these waters they are the algae that take over when diatoms cannot grow, and they are poorly eaten.

flocculation.text: Fine particles and dissolved organic matter clumping together and settling out, which happens abruptly where fresh water meets salt.
flocculation.why: Latin floccus, a tuft of wool. What the clumps look like.

foraminifera.text: Single-celled organisms that build tiny chambered shells. Abundant in sediment, and their shells preserve, which makes them a record of past conditions.
foraminifera.why: Latin foramen (hole) plus ferre (to bear) - the shells are perforated.

frustule.text: The two-part silica shell of a diatom.

glyphosate.text: The world's most used herbicide. Its target enzyme is absent in animals but present in plants, bacteria and fungi, which makes it an antimicrobial as well as a weedkiller.
glyphosate.why: From glycine and phosphonate, its chemical parts.

grab.text: A sampling device dropped to the seabed that bites out a fixed area of sediment and brings it up. One grab is one sample, and it is how nearly all seabed fauna data is collected.
grab.why: It grabs. The fixed area is what makes counts comparable.

Hedley fractionation.text: A sequence of chemical extractions that separates soil phosphorus into pools by how easily it can be released - from immediately available to permanently locked away.
Hedley fractionation.why: The standard soil-science method, and the reason soil scientists never quote total phosphorus alone.

holobiont.text: An organism considered together with all the microbes living in and on it, as one functioning unit - because for many purposes that is what it actually is.
holobiont.why: Greek holos (whole) plus bios. A word that exists because the older picture of an organism turned out to be incomplete.

humus.text: The dark, stable remains of decayed organic matter in soil, after everything easily eaten has gone.
humus.why: Latin humus, ground or earth - the same root as human and humble.

hydrogeology.text: The study of how water moves through rock and soil underground. Nitrogen retention is a hydrogeological quantity as much as a biological one.

hydrophobic.text: Water-repelling. Such substances leave the water and gather at surfaces - which is why they concentrate in the microlayer and in fatty tissue.

hypoxia.text: Not enough oxygen. Conventionally below 4 mg per litre in marine work, with 2 mg/l as severe.
hypoxia.why: Greek hypo- (under) plus oxys, the root in oxygen.

hysteresis.text: A system that does not retrace its path: the conditions that would restore it are not the conditions that broke it. Easy to enter, hard to leave.
hysteresis.why: Greek hysteresis, a shortcoming or lagging behind.

iltsvind.text: Danish for oxygen depletion - literally oxygen-dwindling. The word used in Danish public debate for what happens when the seabed suffocates.
iltsvind.why: Ilt is Danish for oxygen, coined by H.C. Orsted from ild, fire.

immobilisation.text: The opposite of mineralisation: microbes taking dissolved nutrient out of the water or soil to build their own bodies. High-carbon, low-nitrogen material causes it.
immobilisation.why: The nutrient is not destroyed, just made unavailable while it sits inside a bacterium.

in situ.text: In place - an experiment or measurement made where the thing actually lives, rather than in a laboratory.

indsatsbehov.text: Danish for the required effort - the calculated size of the reduction a water body needs to reach its target. The central number of the whole nitrogen policy.

infauna.text: Animals living inside the sediment rather than on top of it - worms, clams, the things a grab sample catches.
infauna.why: Latin in- plus fauna. The ones you have to dig for.

isotherm.text: A curve showing how much of a substance a material will hold at each concentration, measured at one temperature. The standard way to describe a soil's capacity to hold phosphate.
isotherm.why: Greek isos (equal) plus therme (heat) - the temperature is held constant.

Kd.text: The light attenuation coefficient: how fast light dies away with depth. Higher Kd means darker at the bottom.
Kd.why: One broadband number standing in for a whole spectrum, which is why its cause cannot be read off it.

klapplads.text: Danish for a licensed site where dredged material is dumped at sea. There are 114 of them.
klapplads.why: Klappe, to tip or dump; plads, place.

Krebs cycle.text: The central loop of metabolism, by which cells extract energy from food. Present in essentially all aerobic life.
Krebs cycle.why: Hans Krebs, 1937. Also called the citric acid cycle, after the first compound in it.

labile.text: Easily and quickly broken down. Sugars and fresh algal material are labile.
labile.why: Latin labilis, liable to slip or fall. Its opposite here is recalcitrant.

Labyrinthula.text: The slime-mould-like organism that causes eelgrass wasting disease. It destroyed most Atlantic eelgrass in the 1930s and is still present.
Labyrinthula.why: Named for the labyrinth of tracks its cells glide along.

labyrinthulid.text: A group of marine organisms that glide along self-made slime tracks and decompose organic matter - and include the one that causes eelgrass wasting disease. Neither fungi nor animals nor plants.
labyrinthulid.why: Named for the labyrinth of tracks their cells move along. Barely studied, and almost certainly under-appreciated.

Leptosol.text: A very shallow soil, under about 25 cm to rock. Almost no capacity to buffer anything.

Liebig.text: The law of the minimum: growth is set by whichever necessary thing is scarcest, not by the total of everything supplied. Ten nutrients in surplus and one missing gives you no growth.
Liebig.why: Justus von Liebig, the 19th-century chemist who argued it for crops. The name carries none of the meaning, which is why it is worth spelling out.

lignin.text: The rigid material that makes wood woody. It is the hardest common biological molecule to break down, and mainly fungi do it.
lignin.why: Latin lignum, wood. Nitrogen enrichment suppresses the enzymes that degrade it, which is why it accumulates.

lucinid.text: A family of clams that host sulphide-oxidising bacteria in their gills. In seagrass beds they keep the root zone habitable.
lucinid.why: The three-way partnership of plant, clam and bacterium was only described in 2012.

Lysprocent.text: Danish for light percentage - the share of surface light still present at a given depth, already computed in the ODA record. Eelgrass needs roughly 11 to 14 percent.
Lysprocent.why: Lys (light) plus procent. It is the number the eelgrass requirement is written in.

macroalgae.text: Seaweed - algae large enough to see, attached to rock or shell rather than drifting.
macroalgae.why: Macro, large, as against the microscopic plankton.

macrofauna.text: The animals big enough to be caught on a one-millimetre sieve - worms, clams, crustaceans. What a seabed sample is counted as.
macrofauna.why: Macro, large. Below them are meiofauna, below those, microbes.

meiofauna.text: The very small animals between sand grains - nematodes and tiny crustaceans. Too big to be microbes, too small for the sieves used on macrofauna.

mesocosm.text: An experimental container big enough to hold a working piece of an ecosystem, but small enough to control - a tank, an enclosure, a bag in the sea.
mesocosm.why: Greek mesos (middle) plus kosmos (world): between a test tube and the real thing.

mesozooplankton.text: The middle size class of drifting animals, chiefly copepods - between a fifth of a millimetre and two centimetres. The link between algae and fish.

microbiome.text: The community of microbes living in and on an organism, which for many purposes is part of that organism - performing digestion, defence and nutrition it cannot perform alone.
microbiome.why: Micro plus biome. A word that exists because the older picture of an individual organism turned out to be incomplete.

microlayer.text: The top few micrometres of the sea, which concentrate surfactants, fats and hydrophobic pollutants far above their concentration in the bulk water.
microlayer.why: It is the layer a swimmer's skin actually passes through.

micronutrient.text: An element needed in tiny amounts but needed absolutely - iron, zinc, copper, cobalt, molybdenum, selenium. Absence is as fatal as absence of nitrogen.
micronutrient.why: As against macronutrients: carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and the rest needed in bulk.

microphytobenthos.text: Microscopic algae living on the sediment surface. Their secreted polymer glues the grains together and raises the current needed to erode the bed.
microphytobenthos.why: Micro (small) plus phyton (plant) plus benthos (the depths): the tiny plants of the bottom.

mineralisation.text: The breakdown of organic material back into simple inorganic compounds - releasing the nutrients that were locked in tissue.
mineralisation.why: Turning organic matter back into minerals. Remineralisation is the same word for material that was mineral to start with.

mitochondria.text: The compartments in which eukaryotic cells carry out respiration. Descended from captured bacteria, and present in fungi, plants and animals alike - which is why respiratory poisons are rarely selective.
mitochondria.why: Greek mitos (thread) plus chondros (grain), from how they look under a microscope.

mor.text: Raw, matted, unincorporated humus sitting on top of the soil because the fauna that would mix it in are absent or excluded.
mor.why: Also from Danish, meaning mould in the other sense. The terrestrial version of an organic mat on the seabed.

mull.text: Humus that soil animals have worked into the mineral soil - crumbly, fast-cycling, well mixed.
mull.why: From Danish and German muld, mould or loose earth. Its degraded counterpart is mor.

mycobiome.text: The fungal community of a place or a host, as distinct from its bacteria. Marine sediments are turning out to hold far more fungal diversity than anyone expected.
mycobiome.why: Myco (fungus) on the pattern of microbiome. The word is recent because the recognition is recent.

mycorrhiza.text: The partnership between plant roots and fungi that feeds the plant phosphorus in exchange for carbon. Heavy fertilising suppresses it.

målbelastning.text: Danish for target load - how much nitrogen a water body may receive and still meet its environmental objective.

necromass.text: Dead biomass. In soil, dead microbes themselves make up a large share of the lasting organic matter.

nematode.text: A roundworm. In sediment they are microscopic, enormously abundant, and among the last animals left when conditions get bad.

neonicotinoid.text: The most widely used insecticide class. It acts on acetylcholine receptors, which every animal with a nervous system has, including all marine invertebrates.
neonicotinoid.why: Nicotine-like, and acting at the same receptor nicotine does.

nitrate.text: The oxidised, stable form of dissolved nitrogen, and the form that leaches from farmland into groundwater and streams.

nitrification.text: Bacteria oxidising ammonium to nitrate. It consumes oxygen - 4.57 grams per gram of nitrogen - without anything growing.
nitrification.why: From nitre, saltpetre, the old name for nitrate salts.

nitrogenase.text: The enzyme that lets some bacteria pull nitrogen straight out of the air. It requires molybdenum or vanadium, and it is destroyed by oxygen.
nitrogenase.why: The -ase ending marks an enzyme throughout biochemistry.

NOVANA.text: Denmark's national programme for monitoring water and nature. Almost every Danish environmental number ultimately comes from it.
NOVANA.why: Danish acronym: the national programme for monitoring of the aquatic environment and nature.

occlusion.text: Sorbed material becoming physically enclosed inside a mineral, so it can no longer be released at all. The one-way end of sorption.
occlusion.why: Latin occludere, to shut up or close off.

oligotrophic.text: Nutrient-poor, low production, usually clear water.
oligotrophic.why: Greek oligos, few. The other end of the same scale as eutrophic.

oomycete.text: A fungus-like group including Pythium and Phytophthora - water moulds that swim as spores and attack stressed roots. They are not actually fungi despite living like them.

optode.text: An oxygen sensor that measures how a dye's glow is quenched by oxygen. It replaced chemical titration, and the two do not always agree.

overløb.text: Danish for a sewer overflow - untreated sewage discharged directly when rain overwhelms a combined system.
overløb.why: Over plus løb (run). Denmark has 19,665 registered outfall points.

PE.text: Population equivalent - the standard unit of sewage load, one person's daily contribution. Industrial discharges are expressed in how many people they equal.
PE.why: Lets a dairy and a town be added together.

pelagic.text: Of the open water column, as opposed to the bed.
pelagic.why: Greek pelagos, the open sea. Its counterpart is benthic.

peroxidase.text: An enzyme that neutralises reactive oxygen inside a cell. The selenium-dependent version is why selenium is essential.
peroxidase.why: It disposes of peroxides, which would otherwise do damage.

pharmacokinetic.text: To do with how much of a substance an organism takes up, where it goes, and how fast it is broken down - as opposed to what it does once it arrives.
pharmacokinetic.why: Greek pharmakon (drug) plus kinesis (movement). Selectivity that is pharmacokinetic is selectivity of exposure, not of mechanism.

phenology.text: The timing of biological events through the year - when things spawn, bloom, migrate - and whether two events that need to coincide still do.
phenology.why: Greek phainein, to appear. The study of when things show up.

phosphate.text: The dissolved form of phosphorus. It binds tightly to iron oxides in oxygenated sediment and is released again when the sediment loses its oxygen.
phosphate.why: That release is the single strongest feedback loop in a eutrophic system.

photoinhibition.text: Too much light damaging the photosynthetic machinery. The ceiling of the light window.
photoinhibition.why: Light doing the inhibiting - the reason clearest is not always best.

photosystem II.text: The protein complex that splits water and starts photosynthesis. Triazine and urea herbicides block it, which makes them equally effective against algae.
photosystem II.why: The second of two photosystems, named in the order they were discovered rather than the order they act.

Phytophthora.text: A genus of water mould that destroys plant roots. The potato blight that caused the Irish famine was one of these.

phytoplankton.text: The drifting microscopic plants of the water column - diatoms, flagellates, cyanobacteria. Everything else in the sea ultimately eats them or eats something that did.

phytotoxin.text: A substance that poisons plants. Waterlogged ground makes several of its own - organic acids, ethylene, sulphide, and reduced iron and manganese.

picomolar.text: A concentration of one trillionth of a mole per litre. Vitamins and some trace metals matter to marine life at concentrations this small.
picomolar.why: The prefix pico means a trillionth.

picoplankton.text: The smallest plankton, under two thousandths of a millimetre. Too small for most grazers to catch, so what eats them is mostly viruses.
picoplankton.why: Pico, a trillionth - here just meaning very small indeed.

plankton.text: Anything living in the water column that drifts rather than swims against the current, from bacteria to jellyfish.
plankton.why: Greek planktos, wandering. It describes a way of life, not a group of relatives.

polychaete.text: A marine bristle worm. Many build tubes that stabilise sediment; others burrow and mix it. A large share of what a seabed sample contains.

porewater.text: The water in the spaces between sediment grains. Its chemistry is often wholly different from the water above, and it is what a buried animal actually lives in.

priming.text: Adding fresh easily-eaten carbon speeds up the decay of old material that was sitting there stable, because the microbes gain the energy to attack it.
priming.why: As in priming a pump: a small input releases a much larger flow.

propagule.text: Whatever a species uses to start a new individual somewhere else - a larva, a seed, a spore, a fragment.
propagule.why: Latin propagare, to propagate. The unit of arrival.

protist.text: A catch-all for single-celled organisms with a nucleus that are not animals, plants or fungi. Includes most marine algae and many parasites.

pycnocline.text: The depth at which density changes sharply, separating lighter water above from denser water below. It acts as a lid: below it, oxygen is not replaced.

pyrethroid.text: A synthetic insecticide acting on voltage-gated sodium channels - universal in animals. Crustaceans are extremely sensitive, being arthropods like the intended targets.
pyrethroid.why: Modelled on pyrethrins from chrysanthemum flowers.

Pythium.text: A water mould that rots seedlings and roots, thriving where soil or sediment is waterlogged and low in oxygen.
Pythium.why: The classic damping-off disease of a wet greenhouse.

Q10.text: How much faster a biological process runs for every ten degrees of warming. Around two for most decay, meaning respiration roughly doubles.
Q10.why: A rule of thumb old enough to have no better name.

radial oxygen loss.text: Rooted plants leaking oxygen from their roots into the sediment, which keeps sulphide away from the root. It is powered by photosynthesis, so shade shuts it off.
radial oxygen loss.why: Radial because it moves outward from the root, not along it.

recalcitrant.text: Resistant to decay. Lignin, humic material, and most synthetic compounds.
recalcitrant.why: Latin recalcitrare, to kick back - literally to dig the heels in.

Redfield.text: The roughly fixed ratio of carbon to nitrogen to phosphorus in marine plankton, about 106:16:1 by atoms. It lets you convert one nutrient into an expected amount of biomass, or of oxygen demand.
Redfield.why: Alfred Redfield noticed in 1934 that plankton and seawater share the ratio, which is either a coincidence or the plankton setting the chemistry of the ocean.

redox.text: Whether the chemistry of a place is oxidising or reducing - broadly, whether oxygen is available. It governs which reactions run and which metals stay put.

reductase.text: An enzyme that reduces a compound - adds electrons to it. Nitrate reductase is the one that lets an organism use nitrate.
